scope: Theorem 1.1 (Eventually steady forcing) of the manuscript “Universal Computation with Eventually Stationary Navier–Stokes Forcing” (preprints/Universal-Computation-with-Eventually-Stationary-Navier-Stokes-Forcing-September-27-2026/manuscript.pdf), one of the manuscripts of result family 376 of openai/math at commit 1581d4cbdd69. The statement is quoted verbatim from the text that pdftotext 24.02.0 (-raw -enc UTF-8) extracts from the PDF (SHA-256 0af659c5a6f8e7b0), with whitespace normalised, and was found there under this heading on PDF page 2. Text extraction flattens typeset mathematics (superscripts, subscripts, fractions, large operators, delimiters), so the quote can read differently from the typeset statement and can carry characters with no Unicode meaning; the PDF is authoritative. Finding the quote shows that the manuscript states it, not that it is true. AMVO has checked nothing about this claim.
statement: Fix a positive computable viscosity ν. There is an effective procedure taking a deterministic Turing machine and finite input to a body force f on the flat torus 𝕋3, such that: 1. f is smooth on 𝕋3 × [0, ∞), has zero spatial mean, and is independent of time for t ≥ 1. Every spatial, temporal, and mixed derivative of f is bounded on this entire domain. 2. With initial velocity zero, the Navier–Stokes equation has a global smooth solution, unique in the classical class on every finite time interval. Its kinetic energy is bounded uniformly in time. 3. For the fixed particle label and fixed open set P = (1/4, 1/4, 0), 𝒪 = {(X, Y, Z) ∈ 𝕋3 : 1/32 < Y < 1/8}, the material trajectory from P enters 𝒪 at a finite time if and only if the machine halts on the input. The force is specified by a finite formula which does not simulate the chosen execution. The construction is also uniform as a formula in an arbitrary positive parameter ν.
